implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the pattern: a sync.Once value plus once.Do(fn) runs the initialiser exactly once no matter how many goroutines call it, with the happens-before edge the memory model documents for Once, and it replaces the classic 'if cell == nil' guard (which is a data race on both the pointer and the object behind it). Package-level var initialisation plus init() is the eager alternative - ordered within a package, but paid at program start - and is what laziness is chosen against. Keep the Once in a package-level var or behind a pointer: Do serialises all callers while the initialiser runs, so it must be fast or warmed in the background.
pitfalls: sync.Once is not resetable and caches the attempt: if the initialiser's produced value is broken, every later caller receives the broken value - expose an explicit reload path (a mutex plus a generation counter) when that matters.
Copying a sync.Once after first use is a data race (the race detector flags struct copies containing one); keep it in a pointer-receiver struct or a package-level var.

If the initialiser panics, Do considers it to have returned and later calls do not retry - the panic is not re-raised for them, so a partially initialised package can persist; recover inside the initialiser if that is possible.
Do blocks every goroutine that arrives during initialisation (they wait for the first call to finish), which turns a slow initialiser into a latency cliff on the request path.

variants.name: sync.OnceValue / OnceFunc (Go 1.21)
variants.implementation_notes: Go 1.21 added sync.OnceValue, OnceValues and OnceFunc, which wrap the whole pattern into a function value: loadIndex := sync.OnceValue(buildIndex) memoises the first result and returns it on every later call, so there is no exposed flag or cell to get wrong. Use it when the lazily built value is naturally a function result (typically a package-level var initialised from a builder); keep sync.Once when the initialisation is a side effect with no return value distributed across several variables.
pitfalls: Panic behaviour differs from plain Once: OnceValue caches the panic and re-panics with the same value on every call, so a failing initialiser keeps failing loudly (usually preferable, but it cannot be retried).
OnceFunc/OnceValue are typed wrappers and cannot be reset or re-created; for reloads keep a mutex-guarded cell or an atomic.Pointer with an explicit invalidation path.
The wrapped function is only executed on the first call, so any configuration it captures (env vars, files) is frozen for the process lifetime.
